sections.title: Survey Overview
sections.intro: The Solidity Developer Survey 2025 ran for one month and received 640 fully completed responses and 1,095 usable responses after removing empty submissions. Respondents came from 87 countries. Charts use per-question N: every response that answered a given question is included regardless of overall survey completion.

charts.description: India (205), Nigeria (148), and the United States (83) are the top three countries. Respondents also came from Europe, Latin America, and Southeast Asia.
English is the most common native language (346, 34%), followed by Hindi (106), Spanish (74), Portuguese (40), and Russian (38).
74% of respondents are between 18-34. The 25-34 bracket is the largest (38%), closely followed by 18-24 (36%). 9% of respondents are over 45.
57% read/write code professionally. 22% can read/write code but not professionally. 19% are still learning.

The majority are smart contract developers (543, 70%). Auditors/security experts are the second largest group (93, 12%). Researchers (54), fullstack/backend developers (42), and tooling/library developers (25) are also represented.
Crypto is the most common industry (49%), followed by students (18%) and technology (16%).
Professional coding experience varies, with 3-5 years being the most common (23%). 25% have less than a year or no professional coding experience.
Solidity is the most-used language (39%), followed by TypeScript (16%) and JavaScript (13%).
Solidity is the top favorite (32%), followed by Python (16%), JavaScript (11%), and Rust (10%).
Windows (38%), MacOS (31%), and Linux (29%) are the three main operating systems used.
49% of respondents use Solidity daily, 32% weekly. 10% use it rarely or never.
50% of respondents have 0-2 years of Solidity experience. 22% have 2-4 years. 4.5% have used Solidity for more than 8 years.
Self-rated expertise concentrates in the upper range: 7 and 8 are the most common ratings (34% combined). 14% rated themselves as beginners (1), with a separate concentration at that level.
v0.8.x is the most widely used version (86%). Older versions account for 5-8% each (v0.4.x through v0.7.x).
79% get Solidity through a framework. npm (24%) and GitHub releases (16%) are the next most common.

VSCode-based editors (VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf) account for ~80% of usage. Note: the survey grouped these under a single option, so we cannot distinguish between them. Other editors include Vim/Neovim (31), IntelliJ (28), and Zed (17).
Foundry is the most used primary framework (467, 57%). Hardhat v3 (145) and v2 (126) account for 33% combined.
Remix is the most used secondary framework (41% of respondents use it alongside their primary framework).

ethers.js is the most used SDK (609, 70%). viem follows (342, 39%) and wagmi (291, 33%). web3.py (138, 16%) is also used. web3.js has 10 mentions. The library has been deprecated. alloy (54, 6%) is also used, primarily in Rust-based tooling.
v0.8.x is the most widely used version (86%). Older versions account for 5-8% each (v0.4.x through v0.7.x).
34% of respondents rely on compiler support older than the current EVM version (osaka).
Among those who rely on older EVM support, Paris (29), London (25), and Cancun (22) are the most common targets.
45% of respondents don't know what the SMTChecker is. 30% have not used it. 18% have tried it and 7% use it often.
35% of respondents don't know what the IR pipeline is. 28% use it sometimes, 15% use it often, and 22% do not use it.
Among respondents who use the IR pipeline, 39% say it takes too long to compile.
48% of respondents don't know about Sourcify. 28% know about it but don't use it. 23% know about it and use it.
49% don't know what it is. 11% use it.
Ethereum mainnet leads (451, 52%). Base is second (346, 40%), ahead of Arbitrum (305, 35%) and Polygon (263, 30%). 72 respondents (8%) mentioned deploying only to testnets.

43% don't use any other smart contract language. Rust is the most selected alternative (242, 28%). This may reflect cross-ecosystem usage (Solana, NEAR, Stylus) rather than EVM development, as the question did not restrict answers to EVM-compatible languages.
73% report improvement (43% a bit, 31% a lot). 25% reported no change. 2% say it got worse (8 respondents).

Stack too deep errors are the most reported issue (330, 47%). Bytecode size limits (230, 33%) and debugging issues (229, 33%) follow. Optimizer-related issues account for 13% (90). 23% report no recurring issues.
Contracts as objects and inheritance is considered important by 54%, the most frequently selected feature. Unbounded dynamic arrays (34%) and inline assembly (29%) follow.
Top themes from 234 free-text responses: stack too deep (17%), compiler/optimizer issues (14%), array/data structure limitations (11%), bytecode size limit (10%).
24% say the docs are good as-is. The most requested improvement is more real-world examples (23%), followed by proxy/upgrade patterns (11%) and storage/memory layout documentation (11%).

Better gas optimizations is the most requested feature (312, 44%). EIP-712 typehash support (204, 29%) is the second most requested. Reference types in transient storage (164, 23%) and more fine-grained storage layout control (162, 23%) are also among the top requests.

sections.title: Core Solidity
sections.intro: 204 respondents are familiar with Core Solidity (30% of the 678 who reached this question).

charts.description: Among those familiar, better error handling / try-catch replacement (88, 43%) and better delegatecall mechanism / library replacement (83, 41%) are the most selected. 14% selected none.
63% say removing inheritance would cause challenges.
44% estimate the rewrite to type classes/traits would be somewhat difficult, 21% very difficult.
71% of those familiar with Core Solidity say their codebase would benefit from improved compile-time evaluation.
33% are excited/supportive. 21% are skeptical/cautious. 16% are concerned about fragmentation.
58% use AI tools daily. 88% use them at least monthly. 4% don't use AI and don't plan to.
77% of respondents view AI favorably (46% favorable, 31% very favorable). 9% hold unfavorable views. 14% are indifferent.
49% somewhat trust, 30% somewhat distrust, 15% highly distrust, and 6% highly trust AI output.

Testing (61%), documenting code (59%), and learning about codebases (58%) are the top AI use cases. Debugging (53%), auditing (52%), and searching for answers (52%) follow. Writing code (49%) and reviewing code (49%) are somewhat lower.
VSCode (60%), Cursor (32%), and Antigravity (16%) are the top editors used with AI agents.

Claude Code is the most selected preferred assistant (61%), followed by Codex/ChatGPT (16%) and Gemini (10%). Note: this survey was distributed via Solidity community channels, which may introduce distribution bias.

sections.title: Free-Text Feedback
sections.intro: Respondents provided free-text answers to several open-ended questions. Responses were categorized by theme using keyword matching. A single response can match multiple themes.

charts.description: Top themes: Etherscan issues (20%), framework tools (20%), verification flaky/unreliable (15%), no issues (12%).
Main reasons: easier verification (44%), reduced bytecode size (21%), and deterministic/reproducible builds (21%).
Top themes: personal skill growth (38%), better tooling (20%), Foundry improvements (19%), AI tools (16%). Note: 38% of responses described personal skill growth rather than ecosystem improvements.
Top themes: transaction replay/simulation (17%), state inspection (13%), better stack traces (13%), step-by-step debugger (13%), IDE integration (11%).

sections.title: Cross-Analysis
sections.intro: For the cross-analysis charts, self-rated expertise was grouped into three tiers: Beginner (1-4), Intermediate (5-7), and Expert (8-10).

charts.description: Self-rated expertise increases with years of Solidity experience. The most common self-rating of 8+ appears at the 4-6 year mark.
Self-rated Solidity expertise also correlates with general programming experience, though less strongly than with Solidity-specific experience.
Stack too deep is reported by 25% of beginners vs 65% of experts. Bytecode size limit follows a similar pattern (17% vs 47%). Debugging issues are consistent across all levels (29-35%).

Framework choice correlates with expertise level: Remix users are predominantly beginners (60%), Hardhat v3 has the highest share of intermediate users (47%), and Foundry has the highest share of expert users (38%).
Daily AI usage is higher among more experienced respondents: 52% of beginners, 58% of intermediate, and 62% of expert respondents use AI daily.
36% of daily AI users express distrust (somewhat or highly) in the output. Nearly all who highly trust AI (37 of 38) are daily users.
Students cluster at lower expertise (peak at 5), professionals peak at 7-8.
Remix usage is higher among students; Foundry is more common among professionals.
AI adoption is similar between students and professionals.

sections.title: Year-over-Year Comparison
sections.intro:
The 2024 survey received 684 responses compared to 1,095 in 2025. The following highlights the most notable changes between the two years. Some questions changed wording or format between years; where this is the case, it is noted.

Frameworks: Foundry increased from 51% to 57% as the primary framework. Hardhat is at 33% combined in both years, but the 2025 survey distinguished between Hardhat v2 (15%) and v3 (18%). Truffle, which was at 2.4% in 2024, no longer appears in the 2025 results.

Operating system: In 2024, MacOS was the most used OS (43%), followed by Windows (29%) and Linux (28%). In 2025, Windows is the most used (38%), followed by MacOS (31%) and Linux (30%).

Developer experience: DX sentiment is slightly more positive in 2025: 73% report improvement (vs 67% in 2024). The percentage reporting things got worse is unchanged at 1.5%.

Recurring issues: In 2024, stack too deep was reported by 68%, debugging by 55%, bytecode size by 51%, and optimizer issues by 22%. In 2025, these are 47%, 33%, 33%, and 13% respectively. However, the question format changed between years (single multi-select field in 2024 vs separate Yes/No checkboxes in 2025), which may account for some or all of the decrease. The 2025 survey also has a larger and potentially different respondent demographic.

Sourcify and IR pipeline awareness: Sourcify awareness improved: 48% don't know about it in 2025 (vs 56% in 2024), and usage increased from 17% to 24%. IR pipeline awareness also improved: 35% don't know what it is in 2025 (vs 46% in 2024).

sections.title: Methodology
sections.intro:
• Survey ran February-March 2026 using LimeSurvey
  • 1,482 total submissions; 387 responses dropped (empty submissions or those who did not complete any survey page)
  • 640 fully completed (all 8 pages), 1,095 usable (reached page 1+)
  • Free-text "Other" answers were normalized and merged into parent columns
  • Multi-value free-text answers are counted toward each mentioned item
  • Troll/noise entries were filtered out
  • Per-question N is used throughout: each chart shows the number of respondents who answered that specific question
  • Questions marked "conditional" were only shown to respondents who met a prerequisite
